summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client send several commands at once instead of waiting for a reply to each. A server announces that it supports this, which cuts down on network round trips when delivering mail. It replaced RFC 1854 and was itself replaced by RFC 2920.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking one question and waiting for each answer, you hand over a whole list of questions and get the answers back together. Mail gets delivered faster.

questions: how to speed up smtp mail delivery
how does smtp pipelining improve performance
which smtp commands can be pipelined
subtitle: A faster way to send mail by bundling commands together

tldr.problem: SMTP's request-response structure causes delays on high-latency networks, forcing clients to wait for a response after each command before sending the next one.
tldr.mechanism: The server announces support for pipelining with the EHLO PIPELINING keyword, allowing clients to send multiple commands in a batch without waiting for intermediate responses.
tldr.outcome: Mail delivery becomes significantly faster, reducing network round trips from 9 to 4 in typical scenarios, though applications must still check all responses.

today: RFC 2197 defined SMTP command pipelining and was obsoleted by RFC 2920, which provided corrections and clarifications but the core mechanism remains the same.

sections.title: The Problem with SMTP
sections.content: SMTP, the protocol for sending mail, works by sending one command and waiting for a response before sending the next command. This one-request-one-response pattern works fine on fast networks, but on slow or distant links with high latency, the time spent waiting for responses dominates the total connection time. A client might wait for a response 9 times in a single message transaction, even though all the commands are known in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine waiting for each word of an answer before asking the next question, instead of asking all your questions at once.

sections.title: How Pipelining Works
sections.content:
The server announces support for pipelining when the client sends the EHLO greeting command; if the server responds with the PIPELINING keyword, the client knows it can pipeline commands. The client then groups commands into batches and sends them in a single TCP operation without waiting for responses between commands, then reads all the responses at once.

A typical message transaction can be compressed from 9 round trips to 4: the client sends EHLO, then waits once to learn about pipelining; then sends MAIL FROM, all RCPT TO commands, and DATA in one batch; receives all responses; sends the message; and finally sends QUIT.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says 'I can handle pipelined commands', then the client sends all the commands it needs together and waits for all the answers at once.

sections.title: What Commands Can Be Pipelined
sections.content:
Not all commands can be bundled safely. Commands like RSET, MAIL FROM, and RCPT TO can appear anywhere in a pipelined group because they do not change the fundamental state that the client needs to track. However, commands like EHLO, DATA, VRFY, EXPN, TURN, QUIT, and NOOP can only appear as the last command in a group, because their success or failure changes protocol state. The DATA command is critical: it transitions the connection to message content mode, so it must be the final command in its batch.

The client must check the response status for every command in a group; it cannot assume that DATA will be rejected just because all RCPT TO commands failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some commands can go anywhere in a batch of commands, but others (like DATA and QUIT) must be last because they change how the connection works next.

sections.title: What Servers and Clients Must Do
sections.content:
A server that supports pipelining MUST never lose data from the TCP input buffer, even when a command fails. It should respond to the DATA command only if at least one valid RCPT TO address has been received. It MUST NOT buffer responses to state-changing commands like DATA and QUIT, but MAY buffer responses to other commands like RCPT TO, sending them as a unit when convenient. When the TCP input buffer is empty, all pending responses must be sent immediately.

Clients that use pipelining MUST check the status of each command and count responses carefully. The TCP window size (often 4 kilobytes) matters: if a client does not support nonblocking I/O, it must ensure each command group fits entirely within the window to avoid deadlock where the client is waiting to send more commands but has filled the window with unsent data.
sections.plainLanguage: The server must remember everything the client sent, even when commands fail. The client must count all the answers carefully to match them with the commands sent.
